content_metadata.description: A short animated video exploring various methods and scientific studies on happiness, challenging misconceptions about it and offering practical tips for viewers to implement in their daily lives.

qAndA.answer: The narrator considers buying a chocolate bar and a sports car.

qAndA.question: How much caffeine per day does the study on coffee and depression suggest is safe?

activities.description: Narrator introduces the topic of happiness

scenes.contextualRelevance: Implies that societal values often prioritize materialistic pursuits over genuine happiness.

keyMoments.changeDescription: Transition from Curious to Neutral as the background fades to purple and the narrator poses a question.

narrativeProgression.description: Introduces the main topic of the video: what is the most important thing in life?
Video opens with a thought-provoking question: "What's the most important thing in life?"

scenes.title: Introduction

videoEditingDetails.description: Fades from white screen with black tree to intro screen with animation, fades to purple background

activities.description: Narrator explains that happiness isn't about money, fame, or power. Shows people in poverty who are happy.

scenes.contextualRelevance: Contests the notion that material possessions equate to a fulfilling life.

keyMoments.changeDescription: Transitions from Neutral to Happy with the introduction of the word 'Happiness' in bright yellow text and an accompanying smiley face.
Transition to Happy reinforced by the depiction of the kids with ragged clothes jumping and smiling, and the light, cheerful rays emanating from them.

narrativeProgression.description: Challenges the common misconception that happiness is dependent on external factors. Emphasizes the possibility of finding happiness regardless of material wealth.
Narrator introduces examples of happy people living in third-world countries.

props.name: Thought bubbles depicting money, a famous person, a powerful person

scenes.title: Money Doesn't Buy Happiness

videoEditingDetails.description: Smooth transition between concepts, animation of thought bubbles, fade to sunset background

activities.description: Narrator explains a study where people were given money and some spent it on themselves, while others spent it on others. The ones who spent it on others were happier.

characterInteraction.description: The narrator interacts with the Sad Girl by offering her money.

scenes.contextualRelevance: Suggests that acts of kindness and generosity have a positive impact on personal well-being.

keyMoments.changeDescription: Transition to Happy shown through the narrator smiling and holding money while talking about spending money on others.

narrativeProgression.description: Introduces the first tip for increasing happiness: spending money on others. Presents a study demonstrating its effectiveness.
The text "1. Spend Money on Others" appears on screen, introducing the first tip.
Narrator outlines the study's methodology of giving people money to spend on themselves or others.

props.name: Bed, candy shelf, sports car, money, bar graphs

scenes.title: Spend Money on Others

videoEditingDetails.description: Smooth transitions, animation of props. Could trim the scene where the character is lying in bed as it doesn't contribute significantly to the narrative.

activities.description: The narrator explains how listening to sad songs can help you regulate your mood and handle negative emotions.

scenes.contextualRelevance: Challenges the assumption that seeking out only positive stimuli leads to happiness.

keyMoments.changeDescription: Transitions to Happy when the musical note changes from sad to happy, mirroring the narrator's explanation of how sad music can improve mood.

narrativeProgression.description: Presents the second tip for increasing happiness: listening to sad music. Explains that counterintuitively, sad music can help with emotional regulation.
The text "2. Listen to Sad Songs" appears on screen, introducing the second tip.

scenes.title: Listen to Sad Songs

videoEditingDetails.description: Smooth transitions, animation of musical notes and heart changing from sad to happy

activities.description: Narrator explains how studies have shown that drinking coffee can decrease the risk of depression.

scenes.contextualRelevance: Illustrates how seemingly mundane habits can have surprising effects on mental well-being.

narrativeProgression.description: Introduces the third tip for increasing happiness: drinking coffee (in moderation). Highlights research on coffee's potential to reduce depression risk.
The text "3. Drink Coffee" appears on screen, introducing the third tip.
Narrator reveals the key finding: one cup of coffee per day is linked to an 8% decrease in depression risk.

scenes.title: Drink Coffee

videoEditingDetails.description: Smooth transitions, animation of coffee mug and beans.

activities.description: Narrator explains how meditation helps reduce stress and anxiety.

scenes.contextualRelevance: Encourages viewers to explore ancient practices that promote mental well-being.

narrativeProgression.description: Presents the fourth tip for increasing happiness: meditation. Emphasizes the long-standing practice and scientific evidence supporting its benefits.
The text "4. Meditation" appears on screen, introducing the fourth tip.
Narrator points to the extensive history of meditation and its effectiveness in reducing stress.

props.name: Two bald figures in orange and brown clothes sitting in meditation pose, thought bubble

scenes.title: Meditation

videoEditingDetails.description: Smooth transitions, animation of characters meditating.

activities.description: Narrator explains how walking can boost happiness. Show scenes of people walking in nature and in the city.

characterInteraction.description: The boy and girl with backpacks appear together, suggesting they are walking together.

scenes.contextualRelevance: Suggests that engaging with the natural world and physical activity can be sources of joy and well-being.

keyMoments.changeDescription: Transitions to Happy as the scene changes to the boy and girl with backpacks, walking cheerfully in a bright green field.

narrativeProgression.description: Introduces the fifth tip for increasing happiness: going for a walk. Highlights the simplicity and effectiveness of this method.
The text "5. Go for a Walk" appears on screen, introducing the fifth tip.
Narrator mentions that even simply being outside in nature can have a positive impact on mood.

props.name: Sun, clouds, green field, forest, a girl walking in the rain

scenes.title: Go for a Walk

videoEditingDetails.description: Smooth transitions, quick cuts between different walking scenes, fade to black

activities.description: Narrator explains the benefits of expressing one's feelings, talks about a study where participants who wrote about their emotions were more relaxed.

scenes.contextualRelevance: Encourages viewers to process and express their emotions in a healthy way to promote well-being.

keyMoments.changeDescription: Transitions to Calm as the narrator explains the relief that comes from confessing worries and the boy in a blue shirt changes from distressed to smiling.

narrativeProgression.description: Presents the sixth tip for increasing happiness: expressing feelings. Explains that bottling up emotions can be harmful and sharing them can be cathartic.
The text "6. Get Your Feelings Off of Your Chest" appears on screen, introducing the sixth tip.
Narrator references a study showing the calming effects of writing about emotional experiences.

scenes.title: Get Your Feelings Off Your Chest

videoEditingDetails.description: Smooth transitions, animation of thought bubbles, fade to blank screen

activities.description: The Scientist emphasizes that science can help us understand and improve our happiness. The Narrator encourages viewers to subscribe.

scenes.contextualRelevance: Highlights the value of scientific knowledge in understanding and enhancing human well-being.

keyMoments.changeDescription: Transitions to Happy as the narrator emphasizes that science can help us improve our happiness.

narrativeProgression.description: Concludes the video by linking scientific research to the pursuit of happiness.

scenes.title: Science and Happiness

climax.description: The concept of happiness is introduced and contrasted with societal values.

storylines.description: Scenes 1-9 form the main storyline focused on presenting science-backed tips to increase happiness. The climax occurs in Scene 2 (0:27) where the concept of happiness is introduced and contrasted with societal values. This storyline follows a non-narrative structure, offering a collection of facts and tips.

timecoded_text_to_speech.text: What's the most important thing in life?
Contrary to popular opinion, it's not money, fame, or even power.
It's happiness.
This is all you really need to enjoy a high quality of life, plain and simple.
There are plenty of people around the world who live in third world countries with nothing
more than the shirts on their back.
And yet, often these are the happiest people on earth.
This illustrates how you don't need much to be happy.
So what's their secret?
How can you boost your happiness to sky high levels?
Funnily enough, there are plenty of tips and tricks which have been proven to work wonders.
Spend money on others.
When many of us are sad, we often go out and buy something in an effort to cheer ourselves
up.
This could be as simple as a chocolate bar or as extravagant as a new sports car.
But stunning new research has shown that if you really want to use money to increase your
happiness, you need to spend it on other people.
A study from 2008 gave people envelopes full of money.
Half were instructed to spend it on themselves while the other half were instructed to donate
the money to charity or buy a gift for a friend.
Individuals who spent money on others reported much higher levels of happiness.
Listen to sad songs.
When we're feeling blue, many of us put in our headphones, zone out, and play our
favorite music.
But before you choose the happiest songs on your playlist, you might want to listen to
this.
A 2014 study found that those listening to sad music actually received beneficial emotional
effects.
These effects included regulation of negative emotion and mood.
In simpler terms, sad music helps you handle your bad moods.
So if you really want to cheer yourself up, put on the saddest song you can find in your
playlist.
Drink coffee.
We're guessing no one was expecting this one.
There's been a lot of talk about how coffee might be good or bad for you, but not many
people are discussing its effect on mood.
There have actually been a few studies which have looked into this and the results are
pretty stunning.
One of the most interesting studies was published in 2016 and it found that one cup of coffee
per day equated to an 8% decrease in the risk for depression.
Up to a limit of 500 milligrams of caffeine per day.
Why is coffee so good at fighting off depression?
Doctors aren't 100% sure, but they think it might have to do something with antioxidants
and anti-inflammatories present in coffee as well as its link to dopamine production.
Meditation.
Of all the things we're listing here, meditation probably has the most conclusive
signs to back it up.
Meditation has been practiced for thousands of years, long before the signs of psychology
even existed.
People have been aware of its benefits for a very long time and its ability to reduce
stress as well known.
Yes, numerous scientific studies have been able to back this up, proving that there is
a link between meditation and reduced stress and anxiety.
Examples include studies of people in high stress situations such as nursing students or
people who are dealing with the aftermath of Hurricane Katrina.
Meditation worked wonders in almost all situations.
Go for a walk.
Sometimes the simplest methods are often the most effective.
It seems like this is definitely the case when dealing with sadness as research has shown
that merely going for a walk can be a major game changer.
Some studies studied the positive effects of simply getting outside and experiencing nature,
a walk in the forest, for example.
Others found that walking in any situation increased happiness simply because it involved
exercise.
But wherever you choose to stroll, going for a walk seems to be a really good idea to
cheer yourself up.
Get your feelings off of your chest.
Keeping your emotions bottled up inside of you is never a good idea and it definitely helps
to get things off of your chest.
Have you ever felt that massive feeling of relief when you confess your fears and worries?
It really does work wonders and science seems to confirm this.
One recent study looked at how recording a negative emotional experience can actually
help calm our nerves and helps us deal with our worries.
Those who were writing about their emotional experiences were much more calm and relaxed
than those who were writing about other subjects.
As you can see, the cold and calculating laboratories of science can actually teach us a lot
about how to warm up our hearts and cheer ourselves up.
Who knows?
Maybe you'll find yourself using one of these methods one day.

Go to https://audible.com/psych2go or text psych2go to 500 500 for a free 30-day trial and 1 free audiobook

Are you wondering about how happiness could be achieved? Are you jealous of others who's constantly happy, but you yourself can't seem to find happiness? Why can't I be happy, you might ask. Sometimes, depression can be the reason of unhappiness or life stressors, but there are actually ways to make your day better. These include things like doing something nice for someone else, meditation, going for a walk, drinking coffee, expressing yourself, and so forth. 

#psych2go #happiness #researchabouthappiness

Animated by: Ben Carswell 
Check out his animation work here: https://www.youtube.com/Twisted4kStudios

Ben's goal is to one day work as a director for animation. 

These points are researched back so be sure to give the articles below a read: 

Dunn, Elizabeth W., Lara B. Aknin, and Michael I. Norton. "Spending Money on Others Promotes Happiness." Science. March 21, 2008. Accessed September 13, 2018. http://science.sciencemag.org/content/319/5870/1687.

Schroder, Hans S., Tim P. Moran, and Jason S. Moser. "The Effect of Expressive Writing on the Error-related Negativity among Individuals with Chronic Worry." Psychophysiology55, no. 2 (2017). doi:10.1111/psyp.12990.

Taruffi, Liila, and Stefan Koelsch. "The Paradox of Music-Evoked Sadness: An Online Survey." PLOS ONE. Accessed September 13, 2018. https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0110490.

"The Effectiveness of a Stress Coping Program Based on Mindfulness Meditation on the Stress, Anxiety, and Depression Experienced by Nursing Students in Korea." NeuroImage. January 13, 2009. Accessed September 13, 2018. https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0260691708001792.

"Walking for Depression or Depressive Symptoms: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis." NeuroImage. April 04, 2012. Accessed September 13, 2018. https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S1755296612000099.

Wang, L., X. Shen, Y. Wu, and D. Zhang. "Coffee and Caffeine Consumption and Depression: A Meta-analysis of Observational Studies." Current Neurology and Neuroscience Reports. March 2016. Accessed September 13, 2018. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/26339067.
